questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, what happens with this program?
options: It is ill-formed: `std::meta::info` is a consteval-only type, so `r` must be a `constexpr` variable
It compiles and `r` holds a reflection of `int` at run time
It compiles, but `r` holds the null reflection at run time
Undefined behavior: reflections are only valid during compilation
questions.explanation: [basic.types.general] makes `std::meta::info` a consteval-only type. Every object of such a type must belong to a `constexpr` variable, be a template parameter object, or live entirely within one constant evaluation. `r` is an ordinary automatic variable in `main`, so the program is ill-formed, and GCC 16 rejects it. Writing `constexpr std::meta::info r = ^^int;` fixes it. There is no run-time representation of a reflection at all, which is why the "holds a reflection at run time" answer is wrong.

questions.prompt: What does this C++26 program print?
options: Nothing; it is ill-formed because `continue` cannot appear in an expansion statement
Nothing; it is ill-formed because `x` would need a single type for all elements
questions.explanation: `std::tuple` has no `begin` or `end`, so this is a destructuring expansion statement. The body is instantiated once per element, with `x` of type `int`, then `double`, then `char`. In the `double` copy the `if constexpr` branch is taken, and `continue` skips to the next instantiation, which [stmt.cont] allows inside an expansion statement. The output is `1 99 `, with 99 the value of `'c'`. The "single type" answer describes an ordinary range-for, which is exactly what `template for` exists to avoid.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? Compile it with `-std=c++26 -freflection` on GCC 16.
options: Nothing; reading private members through reflection is ill-formed
questions.explanation: Member queries return only the members that are accessible from the given `access_context`. `current()` checks access from `main`, which cannot see the private `b`, so only `a` and `c` are returned. `unchecked()` skips access checking entirely, so all three members are returned. Reflection does not forbid seeing private members, but it makes the caller ask for that explicitly, which is why `3 3` is wrong.

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, what is the result of this declaration?
options: `s` is a `std::string_view` equal to `"int"`
`s` is an empty `std::string_view`
The text of `s` is implementation-defined
It is ill-formed: `identifier_of` throws `std::meta::exception`, so the initializer is not a constant expression
questions.explanation: `identifier_of(r)` throws `std::meta::exception` unless `has_identifier(r)` is true. For a type, `has_identifier` is true only for an unqualified class or enumeration type without template arguments, or a type with a typedef name for linkage purposes. `int` is a keyword, not an identifier, so the call throws, the exception escapes the constant evaluation, and the `constexpr` initializer is ill-formed. The implementation-defined answer describes `display_string_of`, which is the function to use for printable names.

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, what happens with this code?
options: It is ill-formed: `^^int &&` is parsed as a reflection of the type `int&&`
It compiles: `^^Int` reflects the alias, which is a different reflection from `^^int`
The `static_assert` fails, because `^^Int` and `^^int` are equal
It is ill-formed: a type alias cannot be the operand of `^^`
questions.explanation: [expr.reflect] parses a reflect-expression as the longest token sequence that could form one. `^^int &&` is a valid reflect-expression of the type-id `int&&`, so the condition becomes `r != ^^int&& std::meta::is_type_alias(r)`, which is a syntax error. Parenthesizing as `(r != ^^int) && ...` makes it compile. The tempting "It compiles" answer has the right semantics: `^^Int` does represent the alias and compares unequal to `^^int`, and `dealias(^^Int) == ^^int`.

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, is this translation unit well-formed?
options: Yes: `S` becomes an aggregate with one `int` member `x`
Yes, but `S` remains incomplete until the end of the translation unit
No: `data_member_spec` requires the name as a `std::u8string`
No: `define_aggregate` may produce its injected declaration only while evaluating a `consteval` block
questions.explanation: An expression that would produce an injected declaration is not a core constant expression unless it is the expression of a `consteval` block. So the initializer of `r` is not constant, and the declaration is ill-formed. Writing `consteval { std::meta::define_aggregate(^^S, {...}); }` at namespace scope works. The name may be any ordinary or UTF-8 string, so the `u8string` option is wrong. GCC 16 reports "define_aggregate not evaluated from consteval block".

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, which of these declarations is ill-formed?
questions.explanation: A function whose type mentions a consteval-only type must be an immediate function. `a` is declared `consteval`. A specialization of the `constexpr` template `c` and the lambda's call operator in `d` are immediate-escalating, so they become immediate functions automatically. `b` is a plain non-template `constexpr` function, which is never immediate-escalating, so it is ill-formed. GCC 16 says "function of consteval-only type must be declared consteval".

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, what does this program print?
options: Nothing; it is ill-formed because `g` is declared twice with different annotations
questions.explanation: Each annotation, and each instantiation of one, produces a unique annotation, so the repeated `=1` counts twice. For a function, `annotations_of` collects the annotations from every reachable declaration, so the redeclaration adds `=3`. That makes four. The answer `2` assumes annotations deduplicate by value like a set, and `3` forgets one of the two sources. The draft's own example in [dcl.attr.annotation] makes the same point with five annotations.
